payload.goal: An incremental, local, derived index over the WHOLE repo so cross-record questions stop costing O(history) or O(initiative count). Tiered: Tier 0 is a byte-sized hot file (open sessions + held files) making cross-initiative conflict detection O(1) on the shim path; Tier 1 materializes the record graph for structural retrieval — exact, explainable, every result citing the event id that produced it. Maintained by per-initiative cursors so cost is O(new events), never O(history). LOCAL and gitignored: derived state never merges, never syncs, and rebuilds from truth when absent, stale, or corrupt. Zero model calls — the record has recorded edges, so retrieval traverses facts instead of guessing similarity.

payload.because: The log is append-only and ulid-ordered, so any derivation over a PREFIX is permanently valid — an index never needs invalidation, only extension. That makes cost O(new events) instead of O(history), which is the only way a cross-record answer can ever ride a 100ms shim: at 300 initiatives the measured warm sweep alone was 18.9ms and at 1000 it was 64.1ms, both O(initiative count). A MONOLITHIC index was rejected because parsing megabytes to answer a byte-sized question just moves the cost; the hot tier must stay small enough that reading it is free, and richer structure belongs behind an explicit ask. COMMITTING the index was rejected because derived state that merges is a permanent conflict source and a staleness vector across machines — local-only removes both problems at zero cost, since anything derived can be rebuilt. EMBEDDINGS were rejected as the foundation: they need a model (breaking felt-cost D3's zero-API-calls invariant, its cost and privacy guarantees with it) AND they discard the thing that makes this record special — the edges are already recorded facts, so traversal returns exact results that can cite the event id that produced them, where similarity returns guesses that cannot. Auditable retrieval is also what the drift work needs; approximate retrieval would be a new hallucination surface, not a fix for one. node:sqlite was rejected for now because it needs Node >=22.5 against a stated floor of 18; revisit if Tier 1 outgrows flat files.
payload.chose: A TIERED, INCREMENTAL, LOCAL index. Tier 0 is a byte-sized hot file (open sessions and the files they hold) read on the shim path; Tier 1 materializes the record graph for structural retrieval and is read only when asked. Both are maintained by per-initiative cursors (last consumed event id), live under a gitignored .sofar/.index/, and are rebuilt from the logs whenever absent, stale, or unparseable.
payload.over: one monolithic index file, a committed/union-merged index, embeddings-based semantic retrieval, and node:sqlite
payload.rule: The index is derived, never truth: it lives gitignored under .sofar/.index/, is never committed or synced, and any absence, staleness, or corruption must fall back to reading the logs rather than returning a wrong answer.

payload.because: Pure pull puts the strongest protection on the weakest tier, by this project's OWN measurement: the four-cell ladder ranks ruled below ruled+guarded, and "you may query the graph" is a rule. Drift certification exists precisely because instructions get skipped under load, so a cross-initiative safety net that depends on the agent remembering to ask is built on the thing being measured as unreliable. Pull also only ever retrieves KNOWN unknowns — the agent asks about the file it is already thinking about, while the decision that bites is the one it never suspected — and it can fire after the code is written, making it documentation rather than prevention. The push half fixes all three because PostToolUse is mechanical, fires on every edit, and fires at the first moment the path is known. Pull is still necessary and still built: at 300 initiatives nothing can be pushed wholesale, so depth must be on demand. What changes is that the two halves speak with different authority. A guard is relevance the AUTHOR declared ("this applies to these paths") and can be asserted like a standing constraint; adjacency is relevance WE inferred and can only be offered. Collapsing them would manufacture hallucinated relevance — exactly the drift this work exists to remove.
payload.chose: Three layers, split by WHO declared the relevance, and guards built before search. (1) GUARD — PostToolUse asks "does any decision anywhere guard this path" via an O(1) index lookup and surfaces the rule verbatim; pushed by the harness, needing no agent cooperation. (2) PRIME — SessionStart states a concrete fact ("files this initiative touches carry N decisions from M other initiatives, named"), not a capability blurb. (3) QUERY — `sofar find`, agent-initiated, full history for a seed, every result citing the event id behind it.
payload.over: a pure pull design where SessionStart advertises the graph and the agent asks when it judges it needs to, and the original Phase 3 order of building search before guards
payload.rule: Declared relevance (a decision's own guard matching the path) may be ASSERTED to the agent; derived relevance (graph adjacency) may only be OFFERED as worth reading. Never let inferred relevance speak with the authority of a declared rule.

payload.because: A partial index answers "no conflict" for everything it has not built yet, and empty is indistinguishable from safe — exactly the wrong answer D1 forbids. Unlike the warm gate, a build cutoff has no semantic justification: a quiet log provably cannot hold an actively-editing session, but an unbuilt one can. So the cost is paid whole, once per index lifetime, and it buys a steady state that is inside budget at every scale measured: shim end-to-end 60.5ms at 30, 62.1ms at 300, 72.0ms at 1000 initiatives; the derivation itself 1.2/2.0/4.7ms against the fold-every-log path's 4.8/39.9/132.4ms. Context for the one over-budget number: at 1000 initiatives SessionStart already costs 89ms, so that scale is at the edge of the shim budget independent of this work. A background or lazy build is the open door if that ever bites.
payload.chose: The shim REFRESHES Tier 0 on the prompt path and pays a full cold build when the index is absent — 147ms once at 1000 initiatives, over the 100ms budget for that single prompt — rather than bounding the build per invocation.
payload.over: A read-only shim (depends on some other process maintaining the index), a warmth-gated cold build (isWarm costs 46ms at 1000 — more than the read it saves), and a per-prompt build budget that converges over several prompts.

payload.because: Measured at 1000 initiatives, tail reads were 13.1ms of a 15.9ms refresh while stats were 1.8ms — the read was the whole cost, and the reads returned nothing. Neither half of the test stands alone: an append always grows the file, so size catches every append; a rewrite can preserve size, so mtime catches the import/restore/checkout size cannot see. Requiring both means the only undetectable case is a rewrite that forges size AND mtime, which nothing in normal operation does — and the next append to that log restores full corroboration. mtime is a difference detector here, never a warmth signal (warmth.ts rejects it for the opposite reason: git checkout makes cold logs look fresh, which here only ever costs an extra read). Result: refresh went 15.9ms to 4.7ms at 1000, and the version bump makes every v1 cursor cold-start instead of being misread.
payload.chose: Cursors carry mtimeMs (index schema v2): a log whose size AND mtime both match the cursor is skipped without opening it, so a quiet initiative costs one stat.
payload.over: Keeping the v1 cursor and tailing every log every refresh, and skipping on size equality alone.

payload.because: Read frequency is the boundary, exactly as it was in D7. guards.json is read on every edit and holds 3 decisions; graph.json is read once a rule fires and holds the repo's touch history; this is read only on an explicit ask, so it can afford what neither of the others can. At 30/300/1000 initiatives: warm find 2.3/21.4/70.1ms, cold build 17.9/165.2/536.0ms, reach.json 252KB/2.5MB/8.4MB — and the hot halves are untouched at 1000 (Tier 0 3.6ms, guards 3.1ms, priming 14.6ms), because nothing on a shim path imports the module. Growing graph.json instead would have put the whole reach payload on the SessionStart path D10 spent a decision getting to 84.6ms. Prose is CLIPPED because the index exists to say what is worth reading, not to become the thing that is read: a full copy of the record is a copy that invites being read as truth (D1), and every result names the event id, so the record is one command away.
payload.chose: A THIRD Tier 1 half on its OWN cursor — reach.json + meta-reach.json — carrying decision/note prose (clipped to 300 chars), scanned citation handles, and a touch map with the event id of every edge. Refreshed only when someone asks a question.
payload.over: Extending graph.json with event ids and prose (the derived half SessionStart's priming already parses), and building `sofar find` on buildGraph the way `sofar why` and `sofar related` do.

payload.because: An initiative is adjacent to everything inside it, so a corridor through one puts every record two hops from every other and the answer to any question becomes "the repo". That is D9's hub problem — cli/event.ts making the whole repo look adjacent — one level up and structural rather than statistical, so it is fixed structurally rather than by ranking. Dropping initiatives entirely was worse: "which other records are in reach" is the question an agent actually has. Synthesizing the hit from the nearest member answers it with nothing inferred that the member had not already established, and citing the MEMBER's own event keeps the citation inside the log that holds it — carrying the member's reaching edge instead would cite an event in another record, which is no evidence at all that this one holds anything. A test pins it: two records sharing no files stay unconnected at max hops.
payload.chose: An initiative is a DESTINATION, never a corridor: initiative nodes carry no adjacency, a traversal that reaches one stops there, and initiative hits are synthesized from the nearest member reached — citing that member's own event. Only an initiative SEED expands, to what the record holds.
payload.over: Minting initiative↔member edges into the adjacency like every other relationship, or leaving initiatives out of the results entirely.
payload.rule: Never make an initiative node traversable in reach: a traversal may REPORT a record, never continue a path through one.

payload.because: Scanning is lexical and permanent; BINDING depends on which initiatives exist, and `sofar new` changes that answer — a word that qualified nothing yesterday qualifies today, so a handle reading as home-scoped re-binds to another record later. Resolving at index time would freeze the old reading and make the index disagree with the graph permanently, which is the one failure D1 forbids; a test demonstrates the re-binding on a late-arriving slug. The MOVE is what makes it possible at all: the hot-path lock keeps every mcp/ module away from core/graph.ts, and the grammar lived there. Splitting it down is the core/adjacency.ts precedent (record-graph D11) — the shared primitive goes below both readers rather than being copied. Verified against the comparator: the index derives exactly the decision→decision `cites` edges buildGraph derives, 64 for 64 on this record, none missing and none extra.
payload.chose: Citation handles are SCANNED when an event is indexed and BOUND to an initiative at query time, with the grammar split into core/citations.ts BELOW core/graph.ts and re-exported from it unchanged.
payload.over: Resolving a citation to its target when the decision is indexed (the obvious thing — it is a per-event fact), and leaving citation edges out of the index so `find` would call buildGraph for them.

payload.because: A path, slug, session id or handle DENOTES something; words only resemble. Order is the whole safety argument — literal always wins, so `sofar find src/core/graf.ts` can never quietly answer about something else. And a match has no edge: giving it a `via` would dress word overlap up as adjacency the record can prove, which is exactly the authority blur D2 exists to stop. Matches cite the event whose OWN prose holds the words, which is checkable; what they must never claim is that it answers the question.
payload.chose: Lexical seeding is a FALLBACK inside the seed ladder, not a mode: resolveSeed stays literal and unchanged, and resolveQuery consults lexicalSeed only when the literal reading found nothing. A text seed comes back as kind 'text' with its matches on seed.matches, never in groups.

payload.rule: A text match may be OFFERED as prose containing the asker's words, never as an answer, and never as a traversal hit with a via edge.

payload.because: Cursors and derived state live in different files and come apart in ordinary ways: writeIndexMeta lands before the payload write and both fail silently, a cleanup removes one, a partial payload is missing a slug. Every per-tier test wrote both halves together, so nothing caught it — 4.2's damage matrix did, and 28 of its cases fail without the fix. D1 says an absent or corrupt index must fall back to the logs rather than answer wrongly, and answering "this record is empty" is the worst available wrong answer: it reads as "no conflict", "no guard", "nothing adjacent".
payload.chose: A cursor is only meaningful beside the state it produced: when a tier has no prior state for a slug, its cursor is IGNORED and the log is read in full. passOverRecord keys this per slug, so a payload file that is missing, unreadable, or simply lacking a slug the meta still has a cursor for rebuilds that slug from its whole log.
payload.over: Trusting meta.json independently of the payload it describes (what the code did): the pass read only the TAIL into an EMPTY state, wrote that back, and every tier then reported an empty record — stably, until something appended.
payload.rule: Never resume from a cursor whose derived state is absent — state and cursor are two halves of one fact, and either one missing invalidates the other.

payload.because: Reaching the divergence needs a session's registration and its touch to invert in ulid order. Ulids are monotonic within a process; a session's events come from several short-lived ones (the MCP server, each hook shim), so it takes two landing in the SAME MILLISECOND with the random halves falling the wrong way. Measured over this record: 0 of 172 registered sessions. Closing it costs the tier its claim — attributing an unregistered session's touches means STORING them, and the hot file, read on every prompt and bounded today by how many agents are working right now, would carry every touch of every session that never registered (here: 11 sessions, 318 touches). The error also runs toward silence: a held file is missed, never invented, so the advisory conflict line under-reports rather than crying wolf. Only Tier 0 is affected — the derived and reach halves attribute a touch by its own event.
payload.chose: Leave Tier 0 order-sensitive and DOCUMENT the boundary: a file_touched that sorts before its own session_started is not attributed, where the fold attributes it. Stated in SPEC and pinned by a named test rather than left to be discovered.
payload.over: Making Tier 0 order-independent like the fold — holding touches for not-yet-registered sessions and adopting them when the session appears.

payload.note: test/index-equivalence.test.ts: 13 records built append by append, every tier compared to its from-logs comparator as canonical JSON after each one, then answered again under 10 damage modes (130 cases) plus staleness and a no-write-back-into-the-record check. Found and fixed a D1 violation — cursors kept while derived state was deleted made every tier report an empty record, stably (28 of the new cases fail without the fix). Corrected priming-line's expectation, which had pinned that bug as if it were the contract. One divergence documented rather than closed (Tier 0, a touch sorting before its own registration).

plan.goal: An incremental, local, derived index over the WHOLE repo so cross-record questions stop costing O(history) or O(initiative count) — and so point-of-use recall, the drift mechanism already measured to work, stops being confined to one initiative's log. Tier 0 is a byte-sized hot file making cross-initiative conflict detection O(1) on the shim path. Tier 1 materializes the record graph, whose first consumer is CROSS-INITIATIVE GUARDS (pushed by the harness, needing no agent cooperation), then a priming line, then agent-initiated search. Maintained by per-initiative cursors so cost is O(new events). LOCAL and gitignored: derived state never merges, never syncs, rebuilds from truth. Zero model calls — the edges are recorded facts, so retrieval traverses them and cites the event id behind every result.
